intro: In 1947 a shepherd's stone cracked a jar in a cave near the Dead Sea. That jar began a find of about 900 old manuscripts. One small scrap held a line from Deuteronomy 32:8. Its wording did not match the Hebrew Bible most people used. Where the usual text says the nations were divided by the number of the sons of Israel, the scroll says the sons of God.

Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible and its ancient languages, built a large part of his work on that verse. He called his reading the Deuteronomy 32 worldview. In it, God gave the nations to lesser heavenly rulers and kept Israel as his own. In this unit you will follow that idea into Daniel's princes of Persia and Greece, holy ground at Sinai and Zion, and a general who carried Israel's soil home. You will also meet other readers who explain these passages in different ways.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain what a manuscript and a variant are, and compare the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls. You will be able to describe Heiser's reading of Deuteronomy 32, Daniel 10 and 2 Kings 5 in your own words. And you will be able to name at least one other reading of each and compare them fairly.
bigQuestion: How did one verse in the Dead Sea Scrolls shape Michael Heiser's picture of the nations, their gods and the land of Israel, and how do other readers see it?

title: The Gods of the Nations

chapters.title: Deuteronomy 32 and the Dead Sea Scrolls
chapters.bigQuestion: When old copies of the same verse say different things, how do readers decide what the verse first said, and why does it matter?

story.title: A Stone, a Cave and a Broken Jar
story.kicker: In 1947 a young shepherd tossed a stone into a cave and started one of the biggest finds in the study of the Bible.
paragraphs: Early in 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd was looking after goats in the dry hills near the Dead Sea. The land there is rocky and full of caves. According to the best-known telling, one goat wandered off. The shepherd threw a stone into a cave opening. Instead of a thud, he heard something crack. It sounded like pottery breaking.

Later he and his cousins climbed inside. They found tall clay jars. Some held old rolls of leather wrapped in cloth. The rolls were covered in neat lines of Hebrew letters. The young men did not know what they had. They sold the scrolls to dealers in Bethlehem, and the scrolls slowly reached scholars.

The scholars were amazed. One scroll held the whole book of Isaiah. It had been copied more than two thousand years ago. Before this find, the oldest full Hebrew copies of the Bible most people could study were about a thousand years younger. Search teams went back to the hills. Between 1947 and 1956 they found scrolls and scraps in eleven caves near a ruin called Qumran.

Among the tens of thousands of fragments were pieces of the book of Deuteronomy. One small piece held a line from a poem called the Song of Moses. Its wording did not match the Hebrew Bible most people used. That one line, Deuteronomy 32:8, became very important to a scholar named Michael Heiser. This chapter follows that line from the cave to his ideas.
story.think: Why might a copy that is two thousand years old tell readers something that a copy one thousand years old cannot?

lessons.title: What a Manuscript Is
lessons.mainIdea: A manuscript is a copy written by hand, and small differences between copies are called variants.
reading: Before printing presses, every book was copied by hand. A copy written by hand is called a *manuscript*. The word comes from Latin words for "hand" and "written." The people who made copies were called scribes. They wrote with ink on animal skin or on papyrus, a paper made from reeds.

No one has the first copy of any book of the Bible. Those first copies wore out long ago. What survives are later copies, made from earlier copies. Scribes worked very carefully. Still, a tired eye could skip a line or swap one word for a similar one. Sometimes a scribe changed a word on purpose to make the meaning clearer.

A place where manuscripts do not agree is called a *variant*. Most variants are tiny, like a spelling change. A few change the meaning. Scholars who compare manuscripts to learn what a text first said practice *textual criticism*. Here "criticism" means careful judging, not complaining. Heiser used this kind of study often in his work.

words.d: a copy of a text written by hand
a place where two or more copies of a text do not agree
the careful study of manuscripts to learn what a text first said

look.title: Three Copies of One Recipe
look.text: Imagine your grandmother wrote a cookie recipe. Three cousins copied it by hand. Cousin A wrote "2 cups of sugar." Cousin B wrote "2 cups of sugar." Cousin C wrote "1 cup of sugar." The first card is lost. Cousin C also crossed out a word and fixed it.
look.prompt: Which reading would you guess the first card had? What else would you want to know before you decide?

check.q: What is a manuscript?
choices: A book printed on a press
A copy of a text written by hand
check.why: Manuscript comes from Latin words for "hand" and "written." It means a handwritten copy.

check.q: What is a variant?
choices: A kind of paper made from reeds
The first copy of a book
A place where copies of a text do not agree
check.why: A variant is a spot where manuscripts differ, such as a changed word or spelling.

check.q: What does "criticism" mean in textual criticism?
check.why: The reading explains that criticism here means careful judging, not complaining.

lessons.title: The Masoretic Text
lessons.mainIdea: The Masoretic Text is the traditional Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, and its oldest complete copies come from about 900–1000 CE.
reading: Open almost any printed Hebrew Bible today and you are reading the *Masoretic Text*. It is named for the Masoretes. They were Jewish scribes and scholars who worked from about 500 to 1000 CE, mostly in Tiberias, a town in Galilee, and in Babylonia.

The Masoretes did not write a new text. They guarded an older one. Hebrew was written with consonants only. The Masoretes added small dots and marks for *vowels*, so readers would say each word the traditional way. They also added notes in the margins that counted letters and words, to help later scribes copy exactly.

Two famous copies come from this work. The Aleppo Codex was written in about 930 CE. The Leningrad Codex was finished in 1008 CE and is the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives. A codex is a book with pages, not a scroll. Most modern translations, Jewish and Christian, use the Masoretic Text as their main base.

words.d: the traditional Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, guarded and marked by Jewish scribes called Masoretes
sounds like a, e, i, o, u; the Masoretes added dots and marks for them to the Hebrew letters
a handwritten book with pages bound together, instead of a roll

check.q: Who were the Masoretes?
choices: Jewish scribes who guarded the Hebrew text

check.q: What did the Masoretes add to the Hebrew letters?
choices: Marks for vowels and notes in the margins

lessons.title: The Greek Septuagint
lessons.mainIdea: The Septuagint is an old Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Egypt in the 200s BCE, and it sometimes follows a different Hebrew text.
reading: In the 200s BCE, many Jews lived in Alexandria, a large city in Egypt. Their daily language was Greek. Jewish scholars there began translating the Hebrew scriptures into Greek. They started with the Torah, the first five books. Other books followed over the next two centuries or so.

This Greek translation is called the *Septuagint*. The name comes from the Latin word for seventy. An old story, told in a text called the Letter of Aristeas, says about seventy scholars made the translation. Scholars often write it with the Roman numerals LXX, which means seventy.

The Septuagint matters for two reasons. First, it was the Bible of many Greek-speaking Jews, and later of the early church. Writers of the New Testament often quote it. Second, the translators worked from Hebrew copies much older than the Masoretic codices. Where the Greek differs from the Masoretic Text, it can be a clue that the translators' Hebrew copy read differently.

words.d: an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Alexandria, Egypt, in the 200s BCE; written LXX
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Genesis through Deuteronomy

look.title: A Translation as a Witness
look.text: A translator in Alexandria in about 250 BCE has a Hebrew scroll open on a table. She or he writes the Greek words line by line. That Hebrew scroll is later lost. The Greek copy survives. Scholars can work backward from the Greek to guess what the lost Hebrew scroll said.
look.prompt: How can a translation help scholars learn about a Hebrew copy that no longer exists?

check.q: Where was the Septuagint begun?
check.why: Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria, Egypt, began the Septuagint in the 200s BCE.

check.q: Why is it called the Septuagint?
choices: It was finished in the year 70
It was found in seven caves
An old story says about seventy scholars translated it
check.why: The Letter of Aristeas tells of about seventy translators; the name comes from the Latin for seventy.

check.q: Why do scholars compare the Septuagint with the Masoretic Text?
choices: The Masoretic Text was translated from the Greek
The Greek was translated from Hebrew copies much older than the Masoretic codices
The Septuagint was written by the Masoretes
The Septuagint is written in Hebrew
check.why: The Septuagint translators used old Hebrew copies, so differences can show an older Hebrew reading.

lessons.title: Finding the Dead Sea Scrolls
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1947 and 1956, about 900 manuscripts, copied from about 250 BCE to 70 CE, were found in eleven caves near Qumran.
reading: After the first scrolls reached scholars in 1947, the search spread. Bedouin searchers and archaeologists combed the cliffs near *Qumran*, an ancient site by the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. By 1956 they had found writings in eleven caves. Cave 4, found in 1952, held the most, but mostly in small, broken pieces.

Together these finds are called the *Dead Sea Scrolls*. Scholars count roughly 900 different manuscripts, though exact counts vary. They were copied between about 250 BCE and 70 CE. The dry desert air kept the leather and papyrus from rotting away.

About a quarter of the manuscripts are books of the Hebrew Bible. Every book appears except Esther, at least in pieces. Other scrolls are rules for a Jewish community, prayers, commentaries, and books like 1 Enoch and Jubilees. Many scholars link the scrolls to a Jewish group called the Essenes, but others think the scrolls came from several places.

words.d: about 900 ancient Jewish manuscripts, copied about 250 BCE to 70 CE, found in caves near the Dead Sea from 1947 to 1956
an ancient site near the northwest shore of the Dead Sea, beside the caves where the scrolls were found

look.title: Most-Copied Books at Qumran
look.cite: Rounded counts from published lists of the biblical Dead Sea Scrolls; counts vary by scholar
look.prompt: Deuteronomy is the second most-copied book. What does that suggest about how the people who kept these scrolls valued it?

check.q: In which years were the scrolls found in the eleven caves?
check.why: The caves were found between 1947 and 1956. The years 250 BCE to 70 CE are when the scrolls were copied.

check.q: Which cave held the most manuscripts?
check.why: Cave 4, found in 1952, held the most, mostly in small pieces.

check.q: Which of these was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls?
check.why: The caves held copies of Hebrew Bible books like Deuteronomy, and other books like 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

lessons.title: What the Scrolls Showed
lessons.mainIdea: The scrolls showed that the Hebrew text was copied very carefully, and also that more than one form of some books was in use.
reading: Scholars first compared the Great Isaiah Scroll from Cave 1 with the Masoretic Text of Isaiah. The two were about a thousand years apart. Yet they matched closely, apart from spelling and small differences. This showed how carefully scribes had copied the text.

Other scrolls surprised scholars. Some biblical scrolls agree with the Masoretic Text. Some agree with the Hebrew text the Septuagint translators seem to have used. Some agree with neither. So before about 100 CE, more than one form of some books was in use. The Hebrew text had not yet settled into a single form.

This gave textual critics new *evidence*. When the Septuagint differs from the Masoretic Text, a Hebrew scroll sometimes sides with the Greek. That shows the Greek was not just a loose translation. It was following a real Hebrew reading. Deuteronomy 32:8 is one well-known example.

words.d: facts or objects that help show whether an idea is true
a complete scroll of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 1, copied in about 125 BCE

look.title: Three Witnesses
look.text: A verse reads one way in the Masoretic Text (copies from about 1000 CE). It reads another way in the Septuagint (a Greek translation begun in the 200s BCE). A Hebrew scroll from Qumran, about 2,000 years old, agrees with the Septuagint.
look.prompt: Why does the Qumran scroll make scholars take the Septuagint's reading more seriously?

check.q: What did comparing the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic Text show?
choices: The texts matched closely, which showed careful copying
The two had almost nothing in common
The Isaiah Scroll was written in Greek
check.why: Though about a thousand years apart, the two matched closely apart from spelling and small differences.

check.q: What did other biblical scrolls show?
choices: All scrolls matched the Masoretic Text exactly
The Septuagint was copied from the scrolls
Only Isaiah was copied at Qumran
More than one form of some books was in use
check.why: Some scrolls agree with the Masoretic Text, some with the Septuagint's Hebrew, and some with neither.

check.q: Why does it matter when a Hebrew scroll agrees with the Septuagint?
choices: It shows the Greek followed a real Hebrew reading
It shows the scroll was translated from Greek
It proves the Masoretes made mistakes on purpose
It shows the scroll is a forgery
check.why: A Hebrew scroll that matches the Greek shows the translators had a real Hebrew reading in front of them.

lessons.title: The Song of Moses
lessons.mainIdea: In the Masoretic Text, Deuteronomy 32:8 says God set the borders of the peoples by the number of the sons of Israel.
reading: Deuteronomy 32 is a long poem called the *Song of Moses*. In the story, Moses teaches it to Israel near the end of his life. The poem looks back over Israel's history. It praises God as faithful and warns the people not to turn to other gods.

Verses 8 and 9 go back to the distant past. They say that the Most High divided the nations and gave them their inheritance. He set their borders. Then verse 9 says that the LORD's own portion is his people, Jacob. Jacob is another name for Israel. The *Most High* is a title for God.

The key words come at the end of verse 8. In the Masoretic Text, the borders are set "according to the number of the sons of Israel." The King James Version (1611) followed this reading, as did many translations after it. Jewish readers long noticed a link here. Genesis 46:27 says seventy members of Jacob's family went down to Egypt.

words.d: the poem in Deuteronomy 32 that Moses teaches Israel near the end of his life
a title for God in the Hebrew Bible (Hebrew Elyon)
something handed down; in Deuteronomy 32, a nation's land or portion

look.title: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the King James Version
look.text: When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the LORD'S portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 32:8–9, King James Version (1611), following the Masoretic Text
look.prompt: Find the words that tell how the borders were set. Which Hebrew text did the KJV translators follow?

check.q: What is Deuteronomy 32?
choices: A list of laws about food
A poem called the Song of Moses
The story of the Tower of Babel
check.why: Deuteronomy 32 is the Song of Moses, a poem Moses teaches Israel in the story.

check.q: In the Masoretic Text of 32:8, the borders are set by the number of whom?
check.why: The Masoretic Text reads "the sons of Israel," and the KJV follows it as "the children of Israel."

check.q: According to verse 9, what is the LORD's portion?
check.why: Verse 9 says the LORD's portion is his people, and Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.

lessons.title: Angels of God in the Greek
lessons.mainIdea: Most Septuagint manuscripts of Deuteronomy 32:8 read "angels of God," and some read "sons of God."
reading: Now open the Septuagint to the same verse. The first part matches: the Most High divided the nations and set their borders. But the ending is different. Most Greek manuscripts say the borders were set according to the number of the "*angels* of God." A few Greek manuscripts say "sons of God."

Why would a translator write "angels of God"? Many scholars think the translators' Hebrew copy said "sons of God." In the Hebrew Bible, "sons of God" can name heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and Job 38:7. So a translator might explain the phrase for Greek readers by writing "angels."

Now there are two readings. "Sons of Israel" points to a people on earth. "Angels" or "*sons of God*" points to beings in heaven. Those two ideas are very far apart. For a long time, some scholars thought the Greek was just a free translation. A small piece of leather from Cave 4 would change that discussion.

words.d: from the Greek angelos, messenger; in the Bible, heavenly beings sent by God
in the Hebrew Bible, a phrase that can name heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7

look.title: Two Endings Side by Side
look.text: Masoretic Text: the Most High set the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. Septuagint (most copies): the Most High set the borders of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.
look.prompt: One ending points to people on earth and one to beings in heaven. How would each ending change what the verse means?

check.q: What do most Septuagint manuscripts say at the end of Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: Most Greek manuscripts read "angels of God"; a few read "sons of God."

check.q: Which passages use "sons of God" for heavenly beings?
check.why: The reading names Job 1:6 and 38:7, where sons of God are heavenly beings.

check.q: Why might a translator write "angels" for "sons of God"?
choices: Because the Masoretes asked them to
Because Greek has no word for sons
To explain for Greek readers that the phrase meant heavenly beings
check.why: Many scholars think the translators explained "sons of God" as angels, since the phrase can name heavenly beings.

lessons.title: The Scroll from Cave 4
lessons.mainIdea: A Deuteronomy scroll from Qumran Cave 4, called 4QDeut-j, reads "sons of God" in 32:8, and many modern translations now follow it.
reading: Scholars give each scroll a short label. The label 4QDeut-j means: Cave 4, Qumran, Deuteronomy, copy j. This copy is about two thousand years old. Only pieces survive. One piece holds part of Deuteronomy 32:8, and there the Hebrew reads "sons of God."

This *reading* matters. It is in Hebrew, not Greek. So it shows that a Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy really did say "sons of God." It supports the idea that the Septuagint translators had a Hebrew copy like this in front of them.

Many modern English translations now follow the scroll here, not the Masoretic Text. The English Standard Version (2001) reads "sons of God." The New Revised Standard Version (1989) reads "gods." Other translations, such as the King James Version and the Jewish Publication Society's translations, keep "sons of Israel," often with a note.

words.d: a Deuteronomy manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, about 2,000 years old, that reads "sons of God" in 32:8
in textual criticism, the exact wording a particular manuscript has at one spot

look.title: Three Witnesses to Deuteronomy 32:8
rows: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: "sons of Israel"
look.cite: Common scholarly dates for the Leningrad Codex, Codex Vaticanus and 4QDeut-j
look.prompt: Which witness is oldest? Does being oldest settle the question by itself? Why or why not?

check.q: What does the label 4QDeut-j tell you?
choices: It is the fourth chapter of Deuteronomy
It is a Greek copy from Alexandria
It comes from Qumran Cave 4 and is a copy of Deuteronomy
It was the fourth copy found in 1947
check.why: 4Q means Cave 4 at Qumran, Deut means Deuteronomy, and j marks which copy.

check.q: Why is it important that 4QDeut-j is in Hebrew?
choices: It shows the Masoretes wrote it
It shows a Hebrew copy really did read "sons of God"
It proves the Greek was a loose translation
It means the verse was first written at Qumran
check.why: Because the scroll is Hebrew, it shows the "sons of God" reading existed in Hebrew, not only in Greek.

check.q: Which English translation reads "sons of God" in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: The ESV (2001) follows the scroll with "sons of God"; the KJV and JPS keep "sons of Israel."

lessons.title: Why the Readings Differ
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars weigh two main explanations: a scribe changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel," or "sons of Israel" was the older reading.
reading: How did one verse end up with different words? Many textual critics think "sons of God" came first. Later, they suggest, a scribe changed it to "sons of Israel." The phrase "sons of God" might have seemed to give other heavenly beings too much honor. Changing it would protect belief in one God. This idea is a *scribal change* made on purpose.

Other readers defend the Masoretic reading. They point to a *pattern* of seventy. Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations after the flood. Genesis 46:27 says seventy of Jacob's family went down to Egypt. So the nations' number matches Israel's family. Early Jewish teachers and the medieval commentator Rashi read the verse this way.

Michael Heiser thought the case for "sons of God" was strong. He also noticed that texts from Ugarit, an ancient city in Syria, speak of the seventy sons of the god El. To him, that showed a divine family of seventy was a known idea in Israel's world. Other scholars weigh the evidence differently. The debate is still active.

words.d: a change a scribe made to a text on purpose, often to make it clearer or to avoid a meaning that seemed wrong
something that repeats in a way you can notice, like the number seventy in Genesis
an ancient city on the coast of Syria whose clay tablets, found from 1929 on, tell of the god El and his family

look.title: The Number Seventy
rows: Sons of El and Athirat in Ugarit's texts
look.cite: Genesis 10 and 46:27 (Masoretic Text and Septuagint); Ugaritic Baal Cycle (tablet KTU 1.4)
look.prompt: Both sides of the debate use the number seventy. How does each side use it?

check.q: Why might a scribe have changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel"?
choices: To protect belief in one God
check.why: Many textual critics think a scribe changed it because "sons of God" seemed to give other beings too much honor.

check.q: How do defenders of the Masoretic reading use Genesis 46:27?
choices: It lists the sons of El
It says seventy angels guard Israel
It says the scroll was found in Egypt
It says seventy of Jacob's family went to Egypt, matching seventy nations
check.why: Jacob's seventy family members match the roughly seventy nations of Genesis 10.

check.q: What did Heiser notice in the texts from Ugarit?
choices: A list of seventy kings of Israel
Seventy sons of the god El
check.why: Ugarit's texts speak of the seventy sons of El, which Heiser saw as background for "sons of God."

lessons.title: Babel and the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8–9 as a look back at Babel: God gave the nations to lesser divine beings and kept Israel as his own.
reading: Genesis 11 tells of the tower of Babel. People build a tower to reach the heavens. God scatters them and confuses their language. Genesis 10, placed just before it, lists the nations that spread across the earth. Deuteronomy 32:8 also speaks of the Most High dividing the nations. Heiser, like other scholars, linked the two passages.

Heiser read the "sons of God" version this way. At Babel, he argued, God handed the nations over to the rule of lesser heavenly beings, the sons of God. Then God began again with one man, Abraham, in Genesis 12. His family became Israel, the LORD's own portion. Heiser called this the *Deuteronomy 32 worldview*. A *worldview* is a set of big ideas people use to make sense of everything.

Heiser also pointed to Deuteronomy 4:19–20. There Moses says the sun, moon and stars were allotted to the other peoples. But the LORD took Israel out of Egypt to be his own people. To Heiser, this matched 32:8–9. He explained the idea in The Unseen Realm (2015). Other scholars read 4:19 simply as a warning against star worship.

words.d: Heiser's name for the idea that God gave the nations to lesser divine beings at Babel and kept Israel as his own
a set of big ideas that people use to make sense of the world
the city in Genesis 11 where people build a tower and God scatters them and confuses their language

look.title: Heiser on Deuteronomy 32
look.text: Heiser argued that Deuteronomy 32:8–9 describes God dividing the nations at Babel and placing them under lesser divine beings, the sons of God, while choosing Israel as his own people. He believed much of the Old Testament makes more sense with this idea in mind.

lessons.title: Gods Who Were Not Just Statues
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:17 calls the gods Israel turned to shedim, and Heiser argued these were real spirit beings, not only statues.
reading: Later in the Song of Moses, Israel turns away from God. Deuteronomy 32:17 says they sacrificed to *shedim*, not to God. They were gods Israel had not known before, new ones that had come along recently. The King James Version translates shedim as "devils." Many modern translations say "demons."

The Hebrew word shedim is rare. It appears only here and in Psalm 106:37. It seems related to a word for protecting spirits in Akkadian, a language of ancient Mesopotamia. Heiser argued that shedim were real spirit beings. In his reading, they were the powers behind the nations' worship, not just wood and stone.

Other readers take the passage differently. Isaiah 44 mocks idols as blocks of wood that a craftsman carved. Some readers think Deuteronomy 32 means the same thing: the gods were nothing. Heiser answered that the Bible can mock the statues and still treat the powers behind them as real. He wrote about this in Demons (2020).

words.d: a rare Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 106:37 for spirit beings who received sacrifices; KJV "devils"
an ancient language of Mesopotamia, written on clay tablets

check.q: What Hebrew word does Deuteronomy 32:17 use for the beings Israel sacrificed to?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 uses shedim, which the KJV translates "devils."

check.q: What did Heiser argue the shedim were?
choices: Real spirit beings behind the nations' worship
Only statues of wood and stone

choices: As the seventy sons of El

lessons.title: Psalm 96 and Paul
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 96:5 calls the nations' gods elilim, the Greek Septuagint calls them daimonia, and Paul echoes Deuteronomy 32:17 in 1 Corinthians 10:20.
reading: Psalm 96 calls on all the earth to sing to the LORD. Verse 5 says that all the gods of the nations are *elilim*, but the LORD made the heavens. Elilim is a Hebrew word that means worthless things or idols. It sounds a bit like elohim, a word for God or gods. The poet may be making a play on words.

The Septuagint translators chose a different word. In their Greek, the gods of the nations are *daimonia*, the word that later gives English "demons." So the translators read this verse as being about spirit beings. Heiser pointed to choices like this as early evidence for his reading.

The New Testament writer Paul used the same idea. In 1 Corinthians 10:20 he warns that sacrifices to idols are offered to daimonia, not to God. His words echo Deuteronomy 32:17. Many Christian readers see Paul as agreeing with the Song of Moses. Other readers think Paul was warning mainly about sharing in idol feasts, not teaching about spirits.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning worthless things or idols, used in Psalm 96:5 for the gods of the nations
a Greek word for spirit beings; the Septuagint uses it in Psalm 96:5 and Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 10:20
a Hebrew word for God, for gods, or for spirit beings in general

chapters.title: Princes, Gods and Holy Ground
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do some Bible passages link God's people, their worship and their land so closely, and how have readers explained that link?

story.title: Two Loads of Dirt
story.kicker: A foreign general is healed in Israel's river and then asks for a strange gift to take home.
paragraphs: The story is told in 2 Kings 5. Naaman is the commander of the army of Aram, the kingdom north of Israel, with its capital at Damascus. He is brave and respected. But he has a skin disease that will not go away. A young girl from Israel, taken from her home in a raid, works in his house. She tells his wife that a prophet in Israel could help him.

So Naaman travels south with horses, chariots and gifts. He stops at the door of the prophet Elisha. Elisha does not even come out. He sends a messenger with a simple instruction: go wash seven times in the Jordan River. Naaman is angry. Damascus has better rivers, he says. His servants gently talk him into trying. He dips seven times, and his skin becomes like a young child's.

Naaman goes back to Elisha and says that now he knows there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. He offers gifts, but Elisha will not take any. Then Naaman asks for something odd. He asks for as much soil as two mules can carry. He says he will offer sacrifices from now on only to the LORD, the God of Israel.

Why would a general want dirt? He could buy fine things in any market. Readers have puzzled over this request for a long time. Michael Heiser thought the dirt was a clue to how people in the ancient world thought about gods, nations and land. This chapter follows that clue, from a vision in Daniel to a song sung far from home.
story.think: Naaman already said the God of Israel was the true God. Why do you think he still wanted to carry Israel's soil home?

lessons.title: A Vision by the Tigris
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel 10 tells of a heavenly messenger who comes to Daniel by the Tigris River in the time of the Persian king Cyrus.
reading: Daniel 10 opens in the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia. Cyrus had taken Babylon in 539 BCE. In the story, Daniel is an old man by now. He has spent three weeks mourning and fasting. Then, standing by the Tigris River, he sees a man dressed in linen, shining like lightning. Daniel falls to the ground, but the messenger touches him and tells him not to be afraid.

The book of Daniel has two halves. Chapters 1 to 6 are stories about Daniel and his friends in Babylon. Chapters 7 to 12 are visions. A *vision* is a dream or sight full of symbols, here about kingdoms to come. Chapter 10 begins the last and longest vision, which runs to the end of the book.

Readers date the book in different ways. Many Jewish and Christian readers hold the traditional view that Daniel wrote it in the 500s BCE. Many modern scholars think the book was finished in about 165 BCE, when the Greek king Antiochus IV was persecuting Jews in Judea. Either way, the vision looks ahead from Persia to Greece. That matters for the princes in the next lesson.

words.d: in the Bible, a dream or sight, often full of symbols, that a person receives from God
an ancient empire based in what is now Iran; its king Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE

look.title: From Persia to Greece
rows: Antiochus IV persecutes Jews in Judea
look.prompt: Which empire came after Persia? How does this order match the prince of Persia and then the prince of Greece in Daniel 10?

check.q: In whose reign does Daniel 10 take place?
check.why: Daniel 10:1 sets the vision in the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia.

check.q: What do chapters 7 to 12 of Daniel mostly contain?
choices: Visions full of symbols about kingdoms
Songs from the Song of Moses
check.why: Chapters 1–6 are stories; chapters 7–12 are visions about kingdoms to come.

check.q: When do many modern scholars think Daniel was finished?
check.why: Many modern scholars date it to about 165 BCE; traditional readers date it to the 500s BCE.

lessons.title: The Prince of Persia
lessons.mainIdea: In Daniel 10:13 the messenger says the prince of the kingdom of Persia blocked him for twenty-one days until Michael came to help.
reading: The messenger explains why he is late. Daniel's prayer was heard on the first day of his fasting. But "the *prince* of the kingdom of Persia" stood against the messenger for twenty-one days. Those twenty-one days match Daniel's three weeks of mourning.

Then help arrived. *Michael*, "one of the chief princes," came to help the messenger. Michael is one of the few angels in the Hebrew Bible who has a name. In Daniel he is always shown on the side of Daniel's people.

Who is the prince of Persia? He cannot be an ordinary human king. A human ruler could not block a heavenly messenger for three weeks. Also, the verse speaks of "the kings of Persia" as a separate group. So many readers, ancient and modern, think the prince is a heavenly being linked with the nation of Persia.

words.d: in Daniel 10, a leader or ruler; the Hebrew word is sar, also used for officials and army captains
a named angel in Daniel, called "one of the chief princes" and the prince of Daniel's people

look.title: Daniel 10:13 in the King James Version

look.prompt: Find the two princes in this verse. What clue in the verse separates the prince of Persia from the human kings?

check.q: For how long did the prince of Persia withstand the messenger?
check.why: Daniel 10:13 says one and twenty days, matching Daniel's three weeks of mourning.

check.q: Who came to help the messenger?
choices: Michael, one of the chief princes
check.why: Daniel 10:13 says Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help.

check.q: Why do many readers think the prince of Persia is not a human king?
choices: A human could not block a heavenly messenger, and the kings of Persia are named separately
check.why: The prince resists a heavenly messenger, and the verse lists the kings of Persia as a separate group.

lessons.title: Michael, Your Prince
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel 10:20–21 adds a prince of Greece and calls Michael "your prince," and Daniel 12:1 calls him the great prince who stands for Daniel's people.
reading: At the end of chapter 10, the messenger says he will go back to fight the prince of Persia. When he is done, he says, the prince of Greece will come. Greece is the next empire in the vision. In history, Alexander the Great conquered Persia in 331 BCE.

Then the messenger says that no one stands with him in this except Michael, "your prince." The word "your" is plural in Hebrew. It means the prince of Daniel's people, Israel. Daniel 12:1 says it again. It calls Michael the great prince who stands up for Daniel's people in a time of trouble.

Put the pieces together. Persia has a prince. Greece has a prince. Israel has Michael. The book never shows a human battlefield here. It shows a struggle in the *heavenly realm* that runs alongside the rise and fall of empires on earth. Readers have explained that struggle in several ways, as the next section shows.

words.d: the unseen world where the Bible places God, angels and other spirit beings
a group of lands and peoples ruled by one power, like Persia or Greece

look.title: Three Nations, Three Princes

look.prompt: What does this drawing show about how the book of Daniel pictures nations and the heavenly realm?

check.why: Daniel 10:20 says the prince of Greece will come, matching Greece as the next empire.

check.q: Who is "your prince" in Daniel 10:21?
check.why: The messenger names Michael as "your prince," the prince of Daniel's people.

check.q: What does Daniel 12:1 say about Michael?

He wrote the Song of Moses
He is the prince of Greece
He is a king of Persia
check.why: Daniel 12:1 calls Michael the great prince who stands for Daniel's people in a time of trouble.

lessons.title: Heiser's Reading of the Princes
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read Daniel's princes as spiritual rulers over nations, the same beings Deuteronomy 32:8 says God set over the nations.
reading: Heiser connected Daniel 10 to Deuteronomy 32:8–9. Remember his reading of that verse. God divided the nations and set them under the sons of God, but kept Israel as his own. If that is true, Heiser argued, then each nation would have a heavenly ruler. Daniel's prince of Persia and prince of Greece fit that picture.

In Heiser's reading, these rulers had gone wrong. Psalm 82 pictures God standing in the *divine council*, the gathering of heavenly beings, and judging the gods for ruling unjustly. Heiser saw the princes in Daniel as members of that group who now worked against God's plans. He wrote about this in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Angels (2018).

One detail matters for Heiser's reading. Michael is a prince for Israel, but he is on God's side. So Israel's case differs from the other nations. In Deuteronomy 32:9, the LORD himself takes Israel as his portion. Heiser understood Michael as serving God on Israel's behalf, not as a rival god.

words.d: in Heiser's work and in passages like Psalm 82, the gathering of heavenly beings around God
a psalm that pictures God judging the gods, or heavenly beings, for ruling unjustly

look.title: Heiser on the Princes of the Nations
look.text: Heiser taught that the prince of Persia and the prince of Greece in Daniel 10 were heavenly beings who ruled those nations. He tied them to the sons of God of Deuteronomy 32:8 and to the gods judged in Psalm 82.
look.cite: Summary of Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015) and Angels (Lexham Press, 2018)
look.prompt: Name the three passages Heiser linked. How does each one add to the picture?

check.q: Which verse did Heiser connect to Daniel's princes?
check.why: Heiser tied the princes to Deuteronomy 32:8–9, where God sets the nations under the sons of God.

check.q: What does Psalm 82 picture?
choices: God judging the gods for ruling unjustly
check.why: Psalm 82 shows God in the divine council judging the gods.

check.q: How did Heiser understand Michael?
choices: As a rival god to the LORD
As serving God on Israel's behalf
As a human king of Israel
check.why: Heiser saw Michael as on God's side, serving for Israel, since the LORD took Israel as his own portion.

lessons.title: Rulers in Other Jewish Books
lessons.mainIdea: Sirach and Jubilees, two Jewish books from before the time of Jesus, also say God set rulers over the nations but kept Israel for himself.
reading: Heiser was not the first to see rulers over the nations. Other ancient Jewish writers said something like it. *Sirach* is a book of wisdom written in Hebrew in about 180 BCE by a teacher in Jerusalem. It is in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and Protestants place it in the Apocrypha.

Sirach 17:17 says that when God divided the nations of the whole earth, he set a ruler over every people, but Israel is the Lord's portion. The wording sounds very much like Deuteronomy 32:8–9. The writer seems to have read Deuteronomy the way the Septuagint and the Qumran scroll do.

*Jubilees* is a retelling of Genesis and part of Exodus, written in about the 100s BCE. Copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jubilees 15:31–32 says God set spirits over the many nations to lead them astray. But over Israel God set no angel or spirit. God alone is Israel's ruler. Heiser used books like these to show how some Jewish readers understood Deuteronomy 32.

words.d: a Jewish wisdom book from about 180 BCE, also called Ecclesiasticus; in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles
a Jewish retelling of Genesis and part of Exodus from about the 100s BCE, found at Qumran
a group of Jewish books that Protestants keep apart from the Old Testament, though Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include many of them

look.prompt: Compare this with Deuteronomy 32:8–9 from the last chapter. Which reading of 32:8 does Sirach seem to follow?

choices: God set a ruler over every people, but Israel is the Lord's portion

check.why: Sirach 17:17 echoes Deuteronomy 32:8–9: a ruler over each people, Israel the Lord's portion.

choices: God alone, with no angel or spirit set over it
check.why: Jubilees says God set spirits over the nations but set no angel or spirit over Israel.

check.q: Where were copies of Jubilees found?
check.why: Copies of Jubilees were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran.

lessons.title: How Jews and Christians Have Read the Princes
lessons.mainIdea: Many Jewish and Christian readers have seen Daniel's princes as angels of the nations, while others read them as human rulers or as a picture of history.
reading: Later Jewish tradition kept the idea of rulers over the nations. Rabbinic writings, the teachings of Jewish sages collected after about 200 CE, sometimes speak of each nation having a heavenly prince. In Jewish tradition, Michael is often called the *guardian* of Israel. Some later Jewish writers also count seventy nations with seventy angels.

Many Christians have linked Daniel's princes to words in Paul's letters. Ephesians 6:12 speaks of a struggle not against flesh and blood, but against rulers, authorities and powers in the heavenly places. Some Christian readers see Daniel 10 as an early view of the same idea. Heiser read Paul this way too.

Other readers take a different path. Some interpreters have argued that the prince of Persia was a human ruler or official, since sar is a common word for officials. Some modern scholars read the princes as a *symbol*: a way of saying that history is not out of God's hands. These readers agree the passage is about God's care for his people. They differ on the princes.

words.d: someone who watches over and protects; in Jewish tradition, Michael is called Israel's guardian angel
a thing that stands for an idea, like a flag standing for a country
from the rabbis, the Jewish teachers whose sayings were collected in the Mishnah, Talmud and Midrash

look.title: Three Readings of One Prince
look.text: Reader A: the prince of Persia is a heavenly being set over Persia. Reader B: the prince of Persia is a human official at the Persian court. Reader C: the princes are symbols showing that the rise and fall of empires is not beyond God's reach.
look.prompt: Pick one clue from Daniel 10 that each reader might point to. Which clue is hardest for Reader B to explain?

check.q: In Jewish tradition, who is often called the guardian of Israel?
check.why: Jewish tradition often calls Michael Israel's guardian, following Daniel 10:21 and 12:1.

check.q: Which New Testament verse do many Christians link to Daniel's princes?
check.why: Ephesians 6:12 speaks of rulers and powers in the heavenly places, which many Christians link to Daniel 10.

check.q: Why have some interpreters read the prince of Persia as a human official?
choices: Because sar is a common word for officials
check.why: The Hebrew word sar is often used for officials, so some readers take the prince as a human ruler.

lessons.title: The Bush and the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: In Exodus, places where God is present become holy ground, like the burning bush and Mount Sinai.
reading: In Exodus 3, Moses is caring for sheep near Horeb, the mountain of God. He sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. When he turns to look, God calls to him from the bush. God tells him to take off his sandals, because the place where he is standing is *holy ground*.

Holy means set apart for God. The ground is not special because of its rocks. It is holy because, in the story, God is present there. This idea is called *sacred space*. Many ancient peoples believed certain places, often mountains, were where gods lived or met people.

Later, in Exodus 19, the Israelites camp at Mount Sinai, which many readers take to be the same mountain as Horeb. The people must not touch the mountain. Moses sets limits around it. God comes down on the mountain with thunder, cloud and fire, and gives the covenant. Heiser pointed out that the Bible marks such places as God's own ground.

words.d: ground set apart for God because, in the story, God is present there
a place set apart for a god or for worship
the mountain where, in Exodus 19–20, God gives Israel the covenant; also called Horeb

look.title: Exodus 3:5 in the King James Version
look.text: And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
look.prompt: What two things does God tell Moses to do? What reason does the verse give?

check.q: Why is the ground holy in Exodus 3:5?
choices: Because a king built a temple there
Because God is present there in the story
check.why: Holy means set apart for God; in the story the place is holy because God is present.

check.q: What does sacred space mean?
choices: A place set apart for a god or for worship
check.why: Sacred space is a place set apart for a god or for worship.

check.q: What happens at Mount Sinai in Exodus 19?
choices: Daniel sees a man in linen
God comes down on the mountain and gives the covenant

check.why: In Exodus 19–20 God comes down on Sinai with thunder, cloud and fire and gives the covenant.

lessons.title: The Tabernacle and Zion
lessons.mainIdea: The tabernacle carried God's holy presence with Israel, and later Mount Zion in Jerusalem became the main holy place.
reading: Israel could not stay at Sinai forever. So in Exodus 25:8, God tells Moses to have the people make a sanctuary so that he may dwell among them. This was the *tabernacle*, a large tent that could be taken down and carried. Its inner room held the ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest.

Later, King David brought the ark to Jerusalem, and his son Solomon built the temple there. The hill of the temple was called *Zion*. Psalm 48:2 praises Mount Zion as beautiful and the joy of the whole earth. The same verse places Zion "on the sides of the north," in the King James wording.

Heiser noticed something in that phrase. The Hebrew word for north is tsaphon. Zaphon was also the name of a mountain north of Ugarit. In Ugarit's texts, the god Baal lived there. Heiser argued Psalm 48 claims Zion, not Zaphon, as the true home of the true God. Other scholars see a similar borrowing of language, while some read the phrase simply as a direction.

words.d: the tent sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness, where God's presence dwelled in the story
the hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood; also a name for Jerusalem itself
a mountain north of Ugarit that Ugarit's texts call the home of the god Baal; also the Hebrew word for north

look.title: Measuring the Tabernacle
look.prompt: A cubit is about 18 inches. About how many feet long was the courtyard? How would its size compare to a basketball court?

check.q: What was the tabernacle?
choices: A tent sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness
The palace of the king of Persia
check.why: Exodus 25:8 tells Moses to make a sanctuary so God may dwell among the people; this was the tent called the tabernacle.

check.q: What was Zion?
choices: The hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood
check.why: Zion was the temple hill in Jerusalem, praised in Psalm 48.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about Psalm 48:2?
choices: It was copied wrongly by the Masoretes
It claims Zion, not Baal's mountain Zaphon, as the true God's home
check.why: Heiser saw the word tsaphon as a claim that Zion, not Zaphon, is the true God's home.

lessons.title: Naaman's Two Loads of Dirt
lessons.mainIdea: In 2 Kings 5:17, Naaman asks for Israel's soil so he can worship the LORD back home, and Heiser saw this as a sign that land and worship were linked.
reading: Go back to Naaman from the chapter story. After he is healed in the Jordan, he says there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. Then, in 2 Kings 5:17, he asks for two mule-loads of *earth*. He promises to offer sacrifices from now on only to the LORD.

Why soil? Heiser's answer was that, in the ancient world, a land belonged to its god. Aram's land, in this way of thinking, was the territory of other gods. So to worship Israel's God back in Damascus, Naaman would bring a piece of Israel's ground with him. He could stand on it, or build an *altar* on it, as many readers suggest.

Naaman also asks for pardon in 2 Kings 5:18. His king worships in the house of Rimmon, a god of Aram. When the king leans on Naaman's arm there, Naaman must bow too. Elisha answers only, "Go in peace." Readers have long debated what Elisha meant by that. The story shows Naaman as a person working out how to be faithful far from Israel.

words.d: soil or dirt; in 2 Kings 5:17, the ground Naaman carries home from Israel
a raised place, often of earth or stone, where offerings are made
a god worshiped in Damascus, the capital of Aram; named in 2 Kings 5:18

check.q: How did Heiser explain Naaman's request?

lessons.title: David Driven Out
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Samuel 26:19, David says that being driven out of the LORD's inheritance is like being told to go serve other gods.
reading: Before David became king, King Saul chased him through the wilderness. In 1 Samuel 26, David sneaks into Saul's camp at night. He could harm Saul, but he does not. He takes Saul's spear and water jug. Then from a hilltop he calls out to Saul.

In verse 19, David makes a strong complaint. People have driven him out of "the inheritance of the LORD," he says. It is as if they told him, "Go, serve other gods." David is not planning to worship other gods. He is saying that being forced out of Israel's land cuts him off from Israel's God.

Heiser pointed to this verse as another clue. The land of Israel was the LORD's *portion*. Outside it lay lands linked to other gods. So exile from the land meant exile from the LORD's worship. Other readers see David's words as a *figure of speech*: a strong way of saying that he would lose his place at the altar and among God's people.

lessons.title: A Song in a Strange Land
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 137 voices the grief of exiles in Babylon who ask how they can sing the LORD's song in a foreign land.
reading: In 587 or 586 BCE, the army of Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Many people of Judah were taken to Babylon. This time is called the *Babylonian exile*. It lasted until the Persian king Cyrus let exiles return, starting in 538 BCE.

Psalm 137 comes from that time of loss. It pictures the exiles sitting by the rivers of Babylon, weeping as they remember Zion. They have hung up their harps. Their captors ask them to sing one of the songs of Zion. Verse 4 answers with a question: how can they sing the LORD's song in a strange land?

Heiser read the question as more than sadness. For him, it fit the idea that the LORD's worship was tied to his land and his temple. Other readers hear mainly grief and homesickness. Many also note that during and after the exile, Jewish life found new ways to pray and study away from the temple. The *synagogue*, a gathering place for prayer and reading, grew in later centuries.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser saw land and worship as linked by the unseen realm, while other readers point to verses like Psalm 24:1 and see figures of speech or a view that grew over time.
reading: Heiser's view ties many passages together: Deuteronomy 32, Daniel 10, Naaman's soil, David's complaint and Psalm 137. In his reading, the nations belonged to lesser heavenly rulers, while the land of Israel was the LORD's portion. Holy places and holy ground marked where the LORD had placed his name.

Other readers see it differently. Psalm 24:1 says the earth is the LORD's, and everything in it. In Jeremiah 29:7, the prophet tells the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray for it. So some readers say the Bible never limits God to one land. To them, the land passages are *figures of speech* about where Israel's worship and temple were.

Other scholars suggest a *development* over time. In their view, early Israel's language about gods and lands came from its neighbors. Over centuries, they suggest, Israel's writers stressed more and more that there is only one God over all the earth. Heiser disagreed with parts of this view. Readers today can compare the passages and see how each reading handles them.
